content: Calcium oxide (CaO), also known as burnt lime, lime, or quicklime, is a widely utilized chemical compound. It appears as a white, caustic, and alkaline crystalline solid. Commercial lime often contains additional compounds such as magnesium oxide, silicon oxide, and smaller amounts of aluminum oxide and iron oxide. Calcium oxide is typically produced through the thermal decomposition of materials like limestone, which contains calcium carbonate (CaCO₃, also known as calcite). This process, known as calcination or lime-burning, involves heating the material to temperatures exceeding 825°C. During this reaction, a molecule of carbon dioxide (CO₂) is released, leaving behind calcium oxide. This reaction is reversible; once the quicklime cools, it begins to absorb carbon dioxide from the air, eventually converting back into calcium carbonate over time. The calcination of limestone is one of the earliest chemical reactions discovered by humans and was known in prehistoric times. Historically, quicklime was used as a disinfectant, often in a 10% solution called milk of lime. However, it had the drawback of decomposing rapidly when exposed to air and moisture, necessitating the use of fresh, unslaked lime. When converted to hydrated or slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂, also known as portlandite), calcium oxide is used in mortar and plaster to accelerate hardening and improve adhesion. Hydrated lime is easily produced, as lime reacts vigorously with water due to its basic anhydride properties. Lime is also employed in glass production and modern metal industries (e.g., steel, magnesium, aluminum) to remove impurities as slag through its reaction with silicates. In water and sewage treatment, lime is used to reduce acidity, soften water, act as a flocculant, and remove phosphates and other impurities. In papermaking, it dissolves lignin, acts as a coagulant, and is used in bleaching processes. In agriculture, lime improves acidic soils. It is also utilized in pollution control, such as in gas scrubbers to desulfurize waste gases and treat liquid effluents. Traditionally, lime has been used in the burial of bodies in open graves to mask the odor of decomposition. It has also been applied in forensic science to reveal fingerprints. As a refractory and dehydrating agent, lime is used to purify citric acid, glucose, dyes, and as a carbon dioxide absorber. Additionally, it finds applications in pottery, paints, and the food industry. Quicklime has been employed during epidemics, plagues, and disasters to disintegrate bodies and help prevent the spread of disease. It is a key component in the nixtamalization process, which is used to create corn hominy and masa (tortilla dough). Calcium oxide is relatively inexpensive and generates heat energy during its hydration process, as shown in the following reaction: When hydrated lime is heated to redness, calcium oxide is regenerated, reversing the reaction. The hydration process is exothermic, releasing 54 GJ of energy. This property makes it a convenient portable heat source, such as for on-the-spot food warming in self-heating cans. Global lime production is approximately 130 million metric tons annually, with the United States and China being the largest producers, each contributing around 20 million metric tons.
